units.text: INT. SUPERMAN - CONTINUOUS
On the carriage drive in the park of a country house near Richmond a motor car has broken down.

It stands in front of a clump of trees round which the drive sweeps to the house, which is partly visible through them: indeed Tanner, standing in the drive with the car on his right hand, could get an unobstructed view of the west corner of the house on his left were he not far too much interested in a pair of supine legs in blue serge trousers which protrude from beneath the machine.
He is watching them intently with bent back and hands supported on his knees.
His leathern overcoat and peaked cap proclaim him one of the dismounted passengers.
Aha! I got him.
units.name: THE LEGS

units.text: All right now?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: All right now.
units.name: THE LEGS

units.text: Tanner stoops and takes the legs by the ankles, drawing their owner forth like a wheelbarrow, walking on his hands, with a hammer in his mouth.
He is a young man in a neat suit of blue serge, clean shaven, dark eyed, square fingered, with short well brushed black hair and rather irregular sceptically turned eyebrows.
When he is manipulating the car his movements are swift and sudden, yet attentive and deliberate.
With Tanner and Tanner's friends his manner is not in the least deferential, but cool and reticent, keeping them quite effectually at a distance whilst giving them no excuse for complaining of him.
Nevertheless he has a vigilant eye on them always, and that, too, rather cynically, like a man who knows the world well from its seamy side.

He speaks slowly and with a touch of sarcasm; and as he does not at all affect the gentleman in his speech, it may be inferred that his smart appearance is a mark of respect to himself and his own class, not to that which employs him.
He now gets into the car to test his machinery and put his cap and overcoat on again.
Tanner takes off his leather overcoat and pitches it into the car.
The chauffeur (or automobilist or motoreer or whatever England may presently decide to call him) looks round inquiringly in the act of stowing away his hammer.
Had enough of it, eh?
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: I may as well walk to the house and stretch my legs and calm my nerves a little.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Looking at his watch.
I suppose you know that we have come from Hyde Park Corner to Richmond in twenty-one minutes.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: I'd have done it under fifteen if I'd had a clear road all the way.
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: Why do you do it? Is it for love of sport or for the fun of terrifying your unfortunate employer?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: What are you afraid of?
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: The police, and breaking my neck.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Well, if you like easy going, you can take a bus, you know. It's cheaper. You pay me to save your time and give you the value of your thousand pound car.
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: He sits down calmly.
I am the slave of that car and of you too. I dream of the accursed thing at night.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: You'll get over that. If you're going up to the house, may I ask how long you're goin to stay there? Because if you mean to put in the whole morning talkin to the ladies, I'll put the car in the stables and make myself comfortable. If not, I'll keep the car on the go about here til you come.
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: Better wait here. We shan't be long. There's a young American gentleman, a Mr Malone, who is driving Mr Robinson down in his new American steam car.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: springing up and coming hastily out of the car to Tanner.
American steam car! Wot! racin us down from London!
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: Perhaps they're here already.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: If I'd known it!
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: with deep reproach.
Why didn't you tell me, Mr Tanner?
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: Because I've been told that this car is capable of 84 miles an hour; and I already know what YOU are capable of when there is a rival car on the road. No, Henry: there are things it is not good for you to know; and this was one of them. However, cheer up: we are going to have a day after your own heart. The American is to take Mr Robinson and his sister and Miss Whitefield. We are to take Miss Rhoda.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: consoled, and musing on another matter.
That's Miss Whitefield's sister, isn't it?
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: Yes.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: And Miss Whitefield herself is goin in the other car? Not with you?
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: Why the devil should she come with me? Mr Robinson will be in the other car.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: The Chauffeur looks at Tanner with cool incredulity, and turns to the car, whistling a popular air softly to himself.
Tanner, a little annoyed, is about to pursue the subject when he hears the footsteps of Octavius on the gravel.
Octavius is coming from the house, dressed for motoring, but without his overcoat.
We've lost the race, thank Heaven: here's Mr Robinson. Well, Tavy, is the steam car a success?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: I think so. We came from Hyde Park Corner here in seventeen minutes.
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: The Chauffeur, furious, kicks the car with a groan of vexation.
How long were you?
units.name: OCTAVIUS

units.text: Oh, about three quarters of an hour or so.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: remonstrating.
Now, now, Mr Tanner, come now! We could ha done it easy under fifteen.
units.name: THE CHAUFFEUR

units.text: By the way, let me introduce you. Mr Octavius Robinson: Mr Enry Straker.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Pleased to meet you, sir. Mr Tanner is gittin at you with his Enry Straker, you know. You call it Henery. But I don't mind, bless you.
units.name: STRAKER

units.text: You think it's simply bad taste in me to chaff him, Tavy. But you're wrong. This man takes more trouble to drop his aiches than ever his father did to pick them up. It's a mark of caste to him. I have never met anybody more swollen with the pride of class than Enry is.
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Easy, easy! A little moderation, Mr Tanner.
units.name: STRAKER

units.text: A little moderation, Tavy, you observe. You would tell me to draw it mild, But this chap has been educated. What's more, he knows that we haven't. What was that board school of yours, Straker?
units.name: TANNER

units.text: Sherbrooke Road.
units.name: STRAKER
